summary: The Bank of Canada decides on rates this morning with a hike expected, Carney says his Indian Act review may not end in repeal, and EU leaders arrive in Montréal Thursday.
body: The Bank of Canada announces its interest-rate decision at 9:45 a.m. today. In a Reuters poll last week, 19 of 34 economists expected it to raise its key rate by a quarter point to 2.50%, which would be its first rate change in a year [^1]. The reason is prices: inflation rose to 3.1% in September, just above the bank's 1% to 3% target range, and oil near US$117 a barrel has pushed fuel costs up [^1]. A hike would make borrowing dearer for families with variable-rate mortgages, car loans and lines of credit, while growth is already slowing [^1]. The US Federal Reserve also decides this afternoon.

A day after saying he wanted to move "beyond" the Indian Act, Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Tuesday that the review has no "fixed conclusion" and may not end in repeal [^2]. Ottawa will work with First Nations and the provinces on possible replacements [^2]. The 1876 law gives Ottawa broad powers over who has Indian status and what reserves can do; most chiefs see it as outdated, but there is little agreement on whether to scrap it [^2].

On Thursday and Friday, Carney hosts EU Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa in Montréal. They are expected to discuss trade, energy, critical minerals and defence, and a draft statement proposes studying long-term Canadian LNG (liquefied natural gas) exports to Europe [^3].
differences: On the Indian Act, Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew calls the law a "race-based form of identification" that should be abolished, while Carney says the process is open-ended and First Nations views differ [^2].

reads.title: Carney says Ottawa's Indian Act review might not end up abolishing the law
reads.summary: What the Indian Act does, why Carney is now stressing that a review may not end in repeal, and where First Nations leaders and premiers stand.
